title: Technical debt and refactoring
blurb: Define technical debt and refactoring, tell them apart from other agile techniques, and say what happens when debt grows too large.
question: A team has taken shortcuts for three iterations and every new change now takes twice as long. What is this called, what technique improves the structure without changing what the product does, and when does it become a board matter?

teach.h: Two quality techniques that belong together
teach.body: Technical debt is a metaphor, credited to Ward Cunningham, for the eventual consequences of poor system design, architecture or development. Refactoring, defined by Martin Fowler for software, means changing the internal structure of something without changing its external behaviour. Debt describes the problem; refactoring is a way of improving structure. Both are techniques of the quality practice.

teach.h: Debt is unfinished work that charges interest
teach.body: The debt can be seen as work that still needs doing before a job is truly complete. If it is not repaid it keeps accumulating interest, making later changes harder. Unaddressed debt increases disorder in the product and so lowers its overall quality. The term is mostly used in software, but the idea of shortcuts costing more later applies widely.

teach.h: Unpaid debt makes each change slower
teach.caption: Illustration only: the 'interest' on debt shows up as rising effort for each later change.

rows.label: What it is
values: The cost of poor design or shortcuts

teach.body: Although the definition comes from software, PRINCE2 Agile says the same concept can be applied to any product. Reorganizing the chapters of a training manual so it is easier to maintain, while it still teaches exactly the same content, is refactoring. Rewriting it to teach something new is not: that changes external behaviour, so it is new work.

head: Change made
Behaviour changed?
Refactoring?
rows: Split one long code module into three
Reorder a manual's chapters for easier upkeep
Rewrite a course to cover a new topic

teach.h: When does debt become a board matter?

children.label: Manage in delivery
children.sub: teams plan the work to repay it

teach.body: In a PRINCE2 context, tolerances may be applied to technical debt. If the debt is forecast to become too significant, it causes an exception. For example, if accumulated debt means the remaining Must haves cannot be delivered within the stage, the project manager raises an exception report so the board can decide, rather than a highlight, issue or lessons report.

Northwick Building Society's team is building an online mortgage calculator. To hit a demo date, developer Owen Price hard-coded the interest rates. Two iterations later, every rate change needs manual edits in six places: technical debt charging interest. Owen refactors the calculator so rates come from one table; customers see exactly the same results. Project manager Fatima Begum checks the remaining debt against the tolerance agreed for it.

teach.text: Refactoring changes STRUCTURE, not BEHAVIOUR. Technical debt is the accumulated cost of poor design or shortcuts, and it can trigger an exception. Do not confuse either with swarming (the whole team tackles a blocker) or trading (swapping items of similar effort).

items: Refactoring (Martin Fowler): change internal structure without changing external behaviour (9.4.1).
Refactoring can be applied to any product, not only software.
Technical debt (Ward Cunningham): consequences of poor design, architecture or development (9.4.2).
Debt is work still owed before a job is complete; unpaid, it accrues interest.
Debt raises disorder and lowers quality; tolerances may be applied to it.
Debt forecast to become too significant causes an exception: exception report to the board.

summary: You can now define technical debt as the accumulating cost of poor design or shortcuts, and refactoring as improving internal structure without changing behaviour. You can also explain that tolerances can apply to debt and that debt forecast to become too significant causes an exception.

options: Changing a product's external behaviour to meet a new user need
Swapping a new requirement for one of similar effort
Improving internal structure without changing external behaviour
The whole team working together to clear a single blocker
A.why: Refactoring changes a product's internal structure without altering its external behaviour (9.4.1).

whyNot.0: Changing behaviour for a new need is new work, not refactoring.
whyNot.1: Swapping requirements of similar effort is trading.
whyNot.3: The whole team tackling a blocker is swarming.

A.q: What does the technical debt metaphor describe?
options: The eventual consequences of poor design or development
The budget owed to a supplier at the end of a stage
The stories left in the backlog at the end of a release
The cost of the agile coach across several projects
A.why: Technical debt refers to the eventual consequences of poor system design, software architecture or software development (9.4.2).

whyNot.1: Money owed to suppliers is a commercial matter, not technical debt.
whyNot.2: Remaining backlog stories are planned scope, not debt from poor design.
whyNot.3: Coaching costs are project costs, not technical debt.

A.q: Who is credited with the term 'technical debt'?
A.why: PRINCE2 Agile credits the technical debt metaphor to Ward Cunningham (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Martin Fowler is credited with the definition of refactoring.
whyNot.1: Mike Cohn is credited with the term epic user story.
whyNot.2: Jeff Sutherland co-wrote The Scrum Guide with Ken Schwaber.

B.q: A team reorganizes the sections of a staff handbook so it is easier to update, while it still gives exactly the same guidance. What is this?
B.why: Improving internal structure without changing what the product does is refactoring, and the concept applies to any product, not only software (9.4.1).

whyNot.0: Trading swaps a new requirement for an existing one of similar effort.
whyNot.2: Swarming is the team working together on a blocker.
whyNot.3: A/B testing compares two versions with users to see which works better.

B.q: What happens if technical debt is left unpaid?
options: It is written off at the end of the release
It moves to the lessons log for later projects
It accumulates interest, making change harder
It is cleared by the next iteration's demo
B.why: If the debt is not repaid it keeps accumulating interest, making it hard to implement changes later (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Debt does not disappear at a release; it keeps growing until it is repaid.
whyNot.1: Recording a lesson does not remove the debt from the product.
whyNot.3: A demo shows completed features; it does not repay debt.

B.q:
Which two statements are correct?
1. Refactoring can be applied to products other than software.
2. Refactoring changes what users see the product do.
3. Tolerances may be applied to technical debt.
4. Technical debt raises the overall quality of a product.
B.why: Refactoring applies to any product (1), and tolerances may be applied to technical debt (3) (9.4.1, 9.4.2).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: refactoring keeps external behaviour the same.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: unaddressed debt increases disorder and lowers quality.
whyNot.3: Both are wrong: behaviour is unchanged, and debt lowers quality.

C.q: Technical debt has grown so much that the remaining Must haves can no longer be delivered within the stage tolerances. What has occurred, and which product should the project manager send to the board?
options: A status change; a highlight report
C.why: Debt forecast to become too significant causes an exception, and the PM informs the board with an exception report (9.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: An issue report describes one issue's impact; this forecast breach of tolerance needs an exception report.
whyNot.1: A lessons report embeds lessons; it does not ask the board to decide on a breach.
whyNot.3: A highlight report gives regular status, not options for a tolerance breach.

C.q: Which practice includes technical debt among its techniques, and what can be applied to it?
C.why: Technical debt is a quality practice technique, and in a PRINCE2 context tolerances may be applied to it (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Technical debt is described under quality, and the book speaks of tolerances, not risk appetite.
whyNot.1: Debt is a quality technique, and the book does not set a velocity target for it.
whyNot.2: Debt is a quality technique, and a change budget is not what the book applies to it.

C.q: A developer restructures code so that it is easier to maintain, and users see no difference. Which technique is this, and whose definition does PRINCE2 Agile use?
C.why: Changing internal structure without altering external behaviour is refactoring, as defined by Martin Fowler (9.4.1).

whyNot.1: Technical debt is the consequence of poor design, not the act of restructuring.
whyNot.2: TDD writes tests first at unit level; it is not the restructuring described.
whyNot.3: Swarming is the team uniting on a blocker; it is not about restructuring code.

reteach.title: The messy kitchen cupboard
reteach.question: How do the debt and the clean-up relate?

blocks.body: Each time you shove a pan into the cupboard without tidying, you save a minute now. A month later, finding anything takes ten minutes: that is technical debt charging interest. Spending an afternoon reorganizing the cupboard, with all the same pans still in it, is refactoring: better structure, same contents and the same meals.

blocks.text: If behaviour changes, it is not refactoring. If debt is forecast beyond tolerance, it is an exception.

explain.body: Changing the internal structure of a product without changing its external behaviour. Defined by Martin Fowler for software, but applicable to any product.

test.q: Which statement about refactoring is correct?
options: It adds new features for users
It keeps external behaviour the same
It applies to software code but not documents
It replaces the need for testing
test.why: Refactoring improves internal structure without altering external behaviour (9.4.1).

whyNot.0: Adding features changes behaviour, so it is not refactoring.
whyNot.2: The book says the concept can be applied to any product, documents included.
whyNot.3: Refactoring is a structural technique; testing is still needed.

explain.body: The eventual consequences of poor design, architecture or development: work still owed before a job is truly complete. Unpaid, it accrues interest.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. Technical debt can be seen as [?] before a job can be considered complete.
test.why: The debt can be seen as work that needs to be done before a particular job can be considered complete (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Budget approval is a cost matter, not technical debt.
whyNot.1: Estimation is a planning activity, not debt.
whyNot.2: Assessing risks is the risk practice.

explain.body: Unaddressed technical debt increases disorder in the product and so lowers its overall level of quality.

test.q: What effect does unaddressed technical debt have on a product?
options: It lowers the product's overall quality
It raises the team's measured velocity
It reduces the number of user stories
test.why: Unaddressed debt increases disorder and therefore lowers the overall level of quality (9.4.2).

whyNot.1: Timeboxes are fixed and are not shortened by debt.
whyNot.2: Debt tends to slow change, not raise velocity.
whyNot.3: Debt does not reduce the number of stories; it makes them harder to deliver.

explain.body: Tolerances may be applied to technical debt. If the debt is forecast to become too significant, it causes an exception and the PM raises an exception report.

test.q: What does technical debt that is forecast to become too significant cause?
test.why: If the debt is forecast to become too significant, it causes an exception (9.4.2).

whyNot.0: Iterations follow the timebox, not the debt level.
whyNot.2: A forecast breach of tolerance is an exception, not a detail change.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives happen every iteration; they do not handle a tolerance breach.
